disease_info: Posttraumatic Stress Disorder (PTSD) is a trauma- and stressor-related disorder that develops after exposure to actual or threatened death, serious injury, or sexual violence, either directly, as a witness, or through learning about events affecting close others. It is characterized by intrusive re-experiencing of the trauma, avoidance of reminders, negative alterations in cognition and mood, and marked changes in arousal and reactivity, persisting for more than one month and causing significant distress or functional impairment. The clinical course can be acute or chronic, with onset sometimes delayed, and is often complicated by sleep disturbance, irritability, concentration problems, and interpersonal or occupational difficulties. PTSD is distinguished from other anxiety and mood disorders by the requirement for a qualifying traumatic event and the specific pattern of trauma-linked re-experiencing and avoidance.

narrative.stressor: About six months ago, on his way back from an early-morning run along the Salish Sea, Sigfredo was caught in the middle of a shooting outside a late-night bar in Blaine; he dove behind a parked car as someone a few yards away was hit, and he stayed with the injured man until paramedics arrived, with police later calling him as a key witness. Initially he tried to push the experience aside, throwing himself into overtime at the call center, weekend hikes, and cooking for friends, but the incident kept intruding into his daily life and he started quietly avoiding the areas near the bar and late-night outings with his hiking and soccer groups. Over the following four months, his performance at the telecom job slipped—he began making mistakes in CRM entries, dodging Spanish-language calls that reminded him of the police interviews, and putting off his GED prep because he felt "too on edge" to concentrate. He finally went to his community clinic at his mother's urging after his supervisor wrote him up for repeated lateness and he found himself dreading the walk to and from work near the bus stop where the shooting had taken place.
narrative.chief_complaint: “Ever since that shooting, I go out of my way to avoid that whole part of town and anything that reminds me of it, and it’s starting to mess with my job and my life.”

narrative.stressor: Four and a half months ago, during a routine inspection of a partially renovated commercial building, Sherry was inside when an improperly supported section of ceiling collapsed, pinning a contractor nearby and narrowly missing her; she helped direct the rescue while believing for several minutes that the man might die. In the aftermath, her employer and the town paper praised her calm under pressure, and she tried to return to her usual detailed, eco-focused work, but the incident shook the core assumptions she’d built her career on about safety, code compliance, and control. Over the next four months, she began turning down inspections of older or structurally complex properties, spending excessive hours re-checking reports, and arguing with supervisors and contractors over relatively minor risks, which strained her work relationships and left her exhausted by the end of each day. When she started contemplating leaving the inspection field altogether and her husband noticed she was becoming uncharacteristically fearful and rigid about any potential hazards at home, he encouraged her to see a mental health professional through the employee assistance program.
narrative.chief_complaint: “Since that collapse on site, I can’t shake this feeling that buildings are basically unsafe and that I can’t trust my own judgment anymore.”

narrative.stressor: Roughly five months ago, Henry was leading a small commercial wiring job when a junior apprentice accidentally contacted a live high-voltage line; Henry watched him convulse and fall from a ladder, and although the apprentice survived after emergency care, Henry was the one who had to cut the power and start CPR while calling 911. The incident collided painfully with his strong identity as a safety-focused mentor and community-minded tradesman, and after the initial shock wore off, he threw himself into finishing the project and volunteering at his church festival, insisting to coworkers that he was "fine" while privately replaying the scene. Over the next four months, his easygoing banter at job sites faded, he began avoiding certain tasks involving higher voltages, and he snapped at apprentices and friends during pickup basketball, to the point that his foreman pulled him aside about tension on the crew and his best friend stopped inviting him to trivia nights. After he blew up at a younger coworker for a minor mistake and then sat in his parked car shaking instead of going into a new site that reminded him of the accident, he scheduled an appointment with a clinic psychologist recommended by his primary care doctor.
narrative.chief_complaint: “Ever since my guy got shocked on that job, I’ve been flying off the handle over nothing, especially at work, and it’s not like me at all.”
